title: Blocking XPO1 Nuclear Export Promotes Dengue Virus Replication in Cultured Cells - Bioengineer.org

analysis.time: The study was published on November 24, 2026. The experiments were conducted with Huh-7 cells infected with dengue virus type 2 or Zika virus at a multiplicity of infection of five. The time points for analysis were twelve and twenty-four hours post-infection.
analysis.location_and_population: The research was conducted using cultured human Huh-7 cells and neonatal CD-1 suckling mouse brains. The study involved dengue virus type 2 and Zika virus, with the focus on dengue virus as the target entity.
analysis.event: Researchers investigated how blocking the XPO1 nuclear export pathway affects dengue virus replication in cultured human hepatoma cells. They found that inhibiting XPO1 promotes dengue virus replication by altering the subcellular distribution of NS3 and mitochondrial dynamics.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study demonstrated that 17.5% of mitochondria were positive for NS3 gold labeling at twelve hours post-infection, increasing to 27.5% by twenty-four hours. The findings indicate a pro-viral environment in vitro, but no specific case counts, death counts, or risk levels were reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was conducted in vitro using cultured cells and animal tissues. analysis.brief_en: This study, published on November 24, 2026, explores the role of the XPO1 nuclear export pathway in dengue virus replication. Researchers used Huh-7 human hepatoma cells and neonatal CD-1 suckling mouse brains to investigate how blocking XPO1 affects the trafficking of dengue virus non-structural protein 3 (NS3) and its downstream effects on mitochondrial dynamics and innate antiviral defenses. The findings reveal that inhibiting XPO1 promotes dengue virus replication by causing NS3 to accumulate in both the nucleus and mitochondria, reorganizing mitochondrial architecture into elongated networks, and reducing type I interferon secretion. In contrast, Zika virus NS3 did not accumulate in mitochondria under similar conditions. The study highlights the importance of nucleocytoplasmic transport in viral replication and suggests that targeting XPO1 could be a potential strategy for antiviral interventions. However, the research is limited to in vitro experiments and does not provide clinical or epidemiological data on dengue virus outbreaks or public health impacts.
